cases.name: The Orchard Golf & Country Club, Inc., et al. v. Yu and Yuhico
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: On May 28, 2000, members Ernesto Yu and Manuel Yuhico wanted to play golf at the Orchard Golf & Country Club as a pair, but the club's "no twosome" policy barred groups of fewer than three from teeing off on weekend mornings. When the assistant golf director, Francis Montallana, refused to let them play, Yu shouted invectives at him and the two teed off anyway, without permission and without the required tee time slip. After asking for their written comments, the board suspended them for three months. After much litigation over injunctions, the Regional Trial Court of Imus declared the suspension void and awarded each of them ₱2,000,000 moral damages, ₱2,000,000 exemplary damages, attorney's fees and costs; ₱9,200,000 was paid under a writ of execution. The club filed a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review under Rule 43 (as required for intra-corporate cases by A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC), then asked the Court of Appeals for time to file the petition. The Court of Appeals first granted the extension, then reversed itself.
cases.issue: (1) Should the Court of Appeals have allowed the late petition for review? (2) Were Yu and Yuhico entitled to damages for their suspension?
cases.ruling: The Court granted the petition, dismissed the complaints and ordered Yu and Yuhico to return the ₱9,200,000. (1) The rules on the period to appeal are generally inviolable, but may be relaxed to serve substantial justice, especially where the appeal appears meritorious or there are compelling reasons; here the delay was only seven days, the club candidly admitted its mistake, A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC itself allows extensions, and there was no material prejudice. (2) On the merits, the members admitted violating the club's rules, were given notice and opportunity to be heard, and were validly suspended under the by-laws. Their claimed damages were supported only by self-serving declarations. Any damage was damnum absque injuria: injury is the illegal invasion of a legal right, damage is the resulting loss, and damages are the compensation; there must be both a legal wrong and resulting damage. One who makes use of his own legal right does no injury (qui jure suo utitur nullum damnum facit), and the mental anguish, if any, was self-inflicted.
cases.keyDoctrine: Damages are the recompense or compensation awarded for the damage suffered; damage is the loss, hurt or harm resulting from the injury; injury is the illegal invasion of a legal right. To recover damages there must be both a right of action for a legal wrong inflicted by the defendant and damage resulting from it (damnum et injuria). Damage without injury (damnum absque injuria) is not compensable, and one who makes use of his own legal right does no injury. Procedural rules on appeal periods may be relaxed to serve substantial justice.

cases.name: People v. Muyco
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: On the night of May 13, 1995, cousins Jesus and Arnulfo Muyco were drinking with Romeo Boteja, Jr., 19, and Romeo's uncle Ernesto under a mango tree in Cabatuan, Iloilo. Arnulfo suddenly grabbed Romeo's hands and Jesus stabbed him below the collarbone, killing him. Ernesto, frozen with shock, later fled. Only Jesus was caught. He raised alibi, saying he was in Passi, Iloilo, some 50 kilometers away. The trial court convicted him of murder, sentenced him to reclusion perpetua, and ordered him to pay ₱30,000 death indemnity and ₱27,000 funeral expenses, but awarded nothing for loss of earning capacity although the victim's mother testified that he earned ₱1,600 a month as a farm laborer.
cases.issue: (1) Was the conviction for murder proper? (2) Are the heirs entitled to damages for the victim's loss of earning capacity, and how much?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed the conviction with modifications. The eyewitness's failure to react was understandable, since people react differently to startling events, and minor discrepancies strengthen rather than destroy credibility. Alibi failed against positive identification, especially as it was not shown to be physically impossible for the accused to be at the scene. Treachery was present. On damages, the death indemnity was increased to ₱50,000, and the Court awarded loss of earning capacity: following People v. Dizon, documentary evidence is the rule, but testimony suffices when the victim was self-employed or a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage. Using the formula 2/3 (80 − age at death) × (gross annual income − 80% of gross annual income), the heirs of the 19-year-old victim were awarded ₱156,172.80.
cases.keyDoctrine: Lost earnings are computed as: net earning capacity = 2/3 × (80 − age at time of death) × (gross annual income − living expenses of 80% of gross annual income). Documentary evidence is generally required to prove loss of earning capacity, but testimony suffices when the victim was self-employed or a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage. Alibi must show physical impossibility of being at the crime scene.

cases.name: Victory Liner, Inc. v. Gammad, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: On March 14, 1996, a Victory Liner bus bound for Tuguegarao, running at high speed, fell into a ravine in Nueva Vizcaya, killing passenger Marie Grace Pagulayan-Gammad, a 39-year-old Section Chief of the BIR. Her husband and children sued for damages for breach of contract of carriage. Victory Liner's counsel failed to appear at hearings, so it was deemed to have waived cross-examination and the presentation of its evidence. The trial court awarded actual damages, death indemnity, moral and exemplary damages lumped together, compensatory damages for loss of earning capacity, and attorney's fees; the Court of Appeals modified the amounts. Victory Liner argued that its counsel's gross negligence denied it due process, and that the damages were baseless.
cases.issue: (1) Was Victory Liner denied due process by its counsel's negligence? (2) Is it liable for breach of contract of carriage? (3) Were the damages proper?
cases.ruling: The Court partly granted the petition. (1) The negligence of counsel binds the client, except where reckless or gross negligence deprives the client of due process; here counsel filed an answer, a pre-trial brief and a timely appeal, and Victory Liner itself was negligent. (2) A common carrier is presumed at fault when a passenger dies, and the presumption is overcome only by proof of extraordinary diligence, which was not shown. (3) Under Article 1764 in relation to Article 2206, the heirs are entitled to death indemnity (₱50,000), indemnity for loss of earning capacity, and moral damages. But the award for loss of earning capacity was deleted: documentary evidence is required, and the deceased, a BIR section chief, did not fall under the exceptions for low-wage workers; ₱500,000 temperate damages were awarded instead under Article 2224, since loss was shown but not its amount. Moral and exemplary damages cannot be lumped together, having different jural foundations; ₱100,000 each was awarded. Actual damages were reduced to the ₱78,160 supported by official receipts. Attorney's fees of 10% were allowed since exemplary damages were awarded, and interest was imposed following Eastern Shipping Lines.
cases.keyDoctrine: In the death of a passenger, the carrier is liable for death indemnity, loss of earning capacity and moral damages (Arts. 1764 and 2206). Loss of earning capacity needs documentary proof, except for self-employed or daily-wage workers earning below the minimum wage; when loss is shown but its amount cannot be proved, temperate damages may be awarded (Art. 2224). Actual damages require competent proof such as official receipts. Moral and exemplary damages have different bases and must be determined separately.

cases.name: Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: On March 17, 1991, in Gumaca, Quezon, a bus of Philippine Hawk Corporation driven by Margarito Avila hit a motorcycle carrying Silvino Tan and his wife Vivian Tan Lee, and a jeep parked on the roadside. Silvino died; Vivian was injured. Vivian sued the company and the driver for damages based on quasi-delict. The trial court found that the driver, who saw the motorcycle ahead, did not slow down but veered to the left lane, and held him guilty of simple negligence; the company was held solidarily liable for failing to exercise the diligence of a good father of a family in selecting and supervising him. Silvino, who operated a gasoline station, earned about ₱1,000,000 a year, shown by a certificate of creditable income tax withheld. The Court of Appeals affirmed and added temperate damages for the motorcycle, moral damages for Vivian's injuries and civil indemnity, though Vivian had not appealed.
cases.issue: (1) Was the driver negligent, and is the company liable? (2) Could the Court of Appeals award damages that Vivian did not appeal for? (3) Were the damages properly computed?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition with modifications. Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence; the driver saw the motorcycle but did not slow down and veered left. When an employee's negligence causes damage, the employer is presumed negligent in selecting or supervising him and must overcome that by convincing proof; the company's tests covered only driving ability and fitness, and it did not know of the driver's prior sideswiping incidents. Under Section 8, Rule 51, an appellate court may review matters not assigned as errors if necessary for a just decision, so the added damages were proper. Indemnity under Article 2206 is for loss of capacity to earn, computed on net earnings: with documentary proof of a ₱1,000,000 gross annual income, and absent other evidence, necessary business expenses were pegged at 80% and living expenses at 50% of the net, giving ₱1,000,000 for the 65-year-old deceased. Actual damages were limited to receipted amounts (₱127,192.85); temperate damages of ₱10,000 were proper for the motorcycle, since only a job estimate was presented; moral damages for the injuries were reduced to ₱30,000; and ₱50,000 civil indemnity was affirmed.
cases.keyDoctrine: Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence. An employee's negligence raises a presumption that the employer failed in the selection or supervision of employees. Indemnity for loss of earning capacity (Art. 2206) compensates loss of capacity to earn and is computed on net earnings: life expectancy of 2/3 x (80 - age at death) multiplied by the gross annual income less necessary expenses, less living expenses. Actual damages need receipts; a mere estimate may justify temperate damages. An appellate court may consider errors not assigned when necessary for a just decision.

cases.name: People v. Asilan
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: On March 27, 2006, in Sta. Mesa, Manila, PO1 Randy Adovas, a 29-year-old police officer in uniform, was about to handcuff a man when Joseph Asilan came from behind and stabbed him in the back several times; the man being arrested then took the officer's gun and shot him. Adovas died. Two eyewitnesses identified Asilan, who was arrested near the scene. Charged with direct assault with murder, he was convicted of murder qualified by treachery and ordered to pay actual damages, moral damages and civil indemnity; the Court of Appeals affirmed. Asilan attacked the witnesses' credibility, argued that treachery was not shown and was not properly alleged, and that he could only be guilty of homicide. The widow had testified, with documentary proof, that her husband earned ₱8,605 a month.
cases.issue: (1) Was Asilan's guilt for murder proved? (2) What damages are due to the heirs, including loss of earning capacity?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed the conviction for murder and modified the damages. The trial court's assessment of credibility stands; minor inconsistencies enhance credibility; there is no standard reaction to a shocking event; and flight indicates guilt but its converse does not prove innocence. Treachery was present, since the officer was stabbed from behind without warning, and it was alleged in the Information; objections to the Information's sufficiency were in any case waived. Civil indemnity was increased to ₱75,000 and moral damages to ₱50,000, exemplary damages of ₱30,000 were added under Article 2230 because of treachery, and actual damages were fixed at the ₱80,224 shown by receipts. Under Article 2206, the lower courts failed to award loss of earning capacity; computing life expectancy as 2/3 (80 − 29) = 34 years and net income as gross annual income (₱103,260) less 50% living expenses, the Court awarded ₱1,755,420, with 6% interest on all damages from finality.
cases.keyDoctrine: Under Article 2206, the defendant is liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, assessed and awarded in every case unless the deceased had no earning capacity due to a permanent disability not caused by the defendant. The factors are the number of years (life expectancy = 2/3 × (80 − age at death)) and the rate of loss (net income, which is gross income less living expenses). Exemplary damages may be awarded under Article 2230 when the crime is committed with an aggravating circumstance such as treachery.

cases.name: Quirante, et al. v. Intermediate Appellate Court, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Atty. John Quirante represented Dr. Indalecio Casasola in a suit against a building contractor and its surety, PHILAMGEN, and won a judgment for actual, moral and exemplary damages, attorney's fees of ₱30,000 and the ₱120,000 surety bond. While PHILAMGEN's challenge to the judgment was pending in the Supreme Court, Dr. Casasola died. Atty. Quirante then moved in the same case for confirmation of his attorney's fees, claiming an oral agreement with the late Dr. Casasola, allegedly confirmed in writing by the widow and two daughters, under which he would get ₱30,000 if the surety bond was recovered, and any award above the bond would be divided equally among the heirs, himself and Atty. Dante Cruz. The trial court confirmed the fees; the Intermediate Appellate Court set aside the confirmation as premature and held that it could not bind heirs who did not sign.
cases.issue: Was the trial court's confirmation of the attorney's fees proper?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed the Intermediate Appellate Court, with an observation. Counsel may claim attorney's fees either in the very action in which the services were rendered or in a separate action; claiming them in the same action is proper, since the right is an incident of the case and the court is familiar with the lawyer's services, and it avoids multiplicity of suits. The fees claimed here, based on a contract for professional services, differ from attorney's fees as damages under Article 2208, which are awarded to the litigant, not to counsel. But the confirmation was premature: the main case was not yet final, and an attorney's fee cannot be determined until the main litigation is decided and something has been recovered from which the fee is to be paid, especially as the agreement was contingent. The Court rejected, however, the appellate court's holding that the confirmation could not affect non-signatory heirs, since that too should be determined by the trial court after the case is adjudicated.
cases.keyDoctrine: Attorney's fees as damages under Article 2208 are awarded to the litigant, who is the judgment creditor, while attorney's fees for professional services are owed by the client to counsel under their contract. Counsel's claim for fees may be made in the same action or in a separate action, but a fee contingent on recovery cannot be determined until the main litigation has been decided and something has been recovered from which the fee is to be paid.

cases.name: Philippine National Bank v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: A government check for ₱97,650 issued by the Ministry of Education and Culture, payable to F. Abante Marketing and drawn against the Philippine National Bank (PNB), was deposited with Capitol City Development Bank, which sent it through the Philippine Bank of Communications (PBCom) for clearing. PNB cleared the check, but more than two months later returned it and debited PBCom's account, claiming a material alteration of the check's serial number. PBCom debited Capitol's account, but Capitol could no longer debit the payee, which had already withdrawn the money. Capitol sued PBCom, which filed a third-party complaint against PNB. The trial court ordered reimbursement with 12% interest and ₱10,000 attorney's fees; the Court of Appeals ordered PNB to honor the check with interest and to pay the attorney's fees.
cases.issue: (1) Is the alteration of a check's serial number a material alteration? (2) Should the uncorroborated certification of the Ministry be given weight? (3) Was the award of attorney's fees proper?
cases.ruling: The Court affirmed the Court of Appeals except for the attorney's fees, which it deleted. An alteration is material if it alters the effect of the instrument, that is, if it changes the items required to be stated under Section 1 of the Negotiable Instruments Law. A check's serial number is not one of them: the change did not alter the relations of the parties, the drawer, the drawee, the payee or the amount, and the issuing agency was clearly printed on the check. Being an innocent alteration, it gave PNB no right to dishonor the check. The Ministry's certification deserved no weight because its signatory was not presented to identify it. As to attorney's fees, neither lower court explained the award: the discretion to award attorney's fees under Article 2208 demands factual, legal and equitable justification; the reason must be stated in the text of the decision, not only in the dispositive portion, since the award is the exception rather than the rule.
cases.keyDoctrine: The award of attorney's fees under Article 2208 is the exception, not the rule; it demands factual, legal and equitable justification, and the reason must be stated in the text of the decision. An award stated only in the dispositive portion is disallowed. A material alteration is one that changes the items required to be stated under Section 1 of the Negotiable Instruments Law; changing a check's serial number is not material.

cases.name: Eastern Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Two fiber drums of riboflavin were shipped from Japan to Manila on a vessel of Eastern Shipping Lines. On arrival, one drum was found damaged; it then passed through the arrastre operator and the customs broker, and when it reached the consignee, one drum had spillage and adulterated contents. The insurer paid the consignee ₱19,032.95 and, as subrogee, sued the carrier, the arrastre operator and the broker. The trial court held them jointly and severally liable, with legal interest of 12% a year from the filing of the complaint; the Court of Appeals affirmed. The carrier questioned its solidary liability and argued that the interest should run only from the trial court's decision and at 6%, since the claim was unliquidated.
cases.issue: (1) Is the carrier liable for the damage, solidarily with the arrastre operator and the broker? (2) From when does legal interest run on an award for loss or damage, and at what rate?
cases.ruling: The petition was partly granted. When goods arrive damaged, the carrier is presumed at fault, and since it failed to rebut the presumption, its liability was inevitable whether or not others were solidarily liable with it. On interest, the Court reconciled its earlier rulings into rules of thumb: (1) for a loan or forbearance of money, the stipulated interest applies, the interest due itself earns legal interest from judicial demand, and absent stipulation the rate is 12% a year from default (judicial or extrajudicial demand); (2) for other obligations, interest on damages may be imposed at the court's discretion at 6% a year, but not on unliquidated claims until the demand can be established with reasonable certainty: from demand if then reasonably certain, otherwise from the court's judgment, always on the amount finally adjudged; (3) once a money judgment becomes final and executory, the rate is 12% a year until satisfied, that period being equivalent to a forbearance of credit. Applying these, interest was set at 6% from the trial court's decision and 12% from finality.
cases.keyDoctrine: Interest as actual and compensatory damages: for a loan or forbearance of money, the stipulated rate (in writing), or absent stipulation the legal rate from judicial or extrajudicial demand; for other obligations, 6% at the court's discretion, running from demand if the claim is then reasonably certain, or else from the judgment; and from the finality of a money judgment, interest until satisfaction because that period is equivalent to a forbearance of credit. Interest due earns legal interest from judicial demand (Art. 2212). The 12% rates applied in this case were later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013 (BSP Circular No. 799, Nacar v. Gallery Frames); check the current rate.

cases.name: Estores v. Spouses Supangan
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: In 1993, Hermojina Estores agreed in a Conditional Deed of Sale to sell a lot in Naic, Cavite to the spouses Supangan for ₱4.7 million. The contract required her to secure a DAR clearance, move a house off the lot and complete the documents, and gave the buyers the right to demand the return of their down payment if she failed to complete the documents. After almost seven years and ₱3.5 million in payments, she had still not complied. On September 27, 2000, the spouses demanded the return of the ₱3.5 million; she acknowledged it and promised to return it, but did not. In the suit for sum of money, she agreed to return the principal but refused to pay interest, since the contract did not provide for it. The trial court imposed 6% interest and attorney's fees; the Court of Appeals set the 6% to run from the demand and reduced the attorney's fees to ₱100,000.
cases.issue: (1) May interest be imposed though the contract does not stipulate it, and at what rate? (2) Are attorney's fees warranted, and in what amount?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition but modified the award. Interest may be imposed even without stipulation: under Article 2210, interest may in the court's discretion be allowed on damages for breach of contract, and the seller, who used the money and failed to return it, was in default from the demand on September 27, 2000. The rate is 12%, because the transaction was a forbearance of money: the phrase "forbearance of money, goods or credits" has a meaning separate from a loan and covers arrangements where a person acquiesces to the temporary use of his money pending the happening of certain events or the fulfillment of conditions. The buyers parted with their money before the conditions were fulfilled, and the seller's unwarranted withholding of it amounts to an involuntary loan. Eastern Shipping and Reformina involved torts, with no forbearance and damages not reasonably certain at demand. The 12% runs from the demand until full satisfaction. Attorney's fees were warranted because the buyers were compelled to litigate, but were reduced to ₱50,000, since they must always be reasonable.
cases.keyDoctrine: Interest may be awarded on damages for breach of contract even without a stipulation (Art. 2210), from default upon demand. "Forbearance of money, goods or credits" is distinct from a loan: it covers arrangements where a person acquiesces to the temporary use of his money pending the happening of events or the fulfillment of conditions; the unwarranted withholding of money that should be returned is a forbearance, an involuntary loan. Attorney's fees under Art. 2208 must always be reasonable. (The 12% rate then applied to forbearances was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013; check the current rate.)

cases.name: Sunga-Chan, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Lamberto Chua and Jacinto Sunga formed a partnership in 1977 to market liquefied petroleum gas under the name Shellite, registered as Jacinto's sole proprietorship. After Jacinto died, his widow Cecilia and daughter Lilibeth Sunga-Chan continued the business without Chua's consent and ignored his demands for accounting and winding up. Chua sued and won: a final judgment ordered an accounting, the return of his one-half share of the partnership assets, unreceived profits of ₱35,000 a month "with legal rate of interest until fully paid", and damages and fees; it became final on December 20, 2001. In execution, the trial court approved Chua's computation of ₱8,733,644.75, which added 12% interest to his share of the assets and to the profits. Lilibeth's property was levied and sold to Chua for ₱8 million.
cases.issue: (1) Was the interest added to Chua's claims proper, and at what rates? (2) Is the petitioners' liability solidary? (3) May the absolute community property of Lilibeth and her husband answer for the judgment?
cases.ruling: The petition was partly granted. Applying the Eastern Shipping rules, the unreceived profits earn 6% from the trial court's decision (October 7, 1997) to its finality (December 20, 2001), and then, with the added interest, 12% from finality until paid, as the award is by then equivalent to a forbearance of credit; the goodwill value and the damages and fees earn 12% from finality. But Chua's one-half share of the partnership assets was an unliquidated claim that earns no interest until reasonably determined: the norm is "reasonably determinable", not determinable by mathematical computation. Since the judgment itself required an accounting and inventory, his share became liquidated only when the trial court approved the accounting, so no interest attaches to it. Chua's claim was reduced to ₱5,529,392.52, and he must pay the excess of his ₱8 million bid. The obligation is solidary because the acts complained of were not severable, the duty to account was indivisible, and the petitioners resisted a legitimate claim in bad faith; and the absolute community may answer for debts contracted by one spouse to the extent the family benefited.
cases.keyDoctrine: Interest does not run on an unliquidated claim until it is reasonably determinable, which is not the same as determinable by mathematical computation; a share that can be fixed only after an accounting becomes liquidated only when the accounting is approved. Under the Eastern Shipping rules, an award not involving a loan or forbearance earns 6% from the judgment, and from finality the award (with the interest added) earns the forbearance rate until satisfied. (The 12% rate was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013; check the current rate.)

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Define damages, and distinguish damages from damage and from injury. Can there be damage without injury? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Injury is the illegal invasion of a legal right; damage is the loss, hurt or harm which results from the injury; and damages are the recompense or compensation awarded for the damage suffered. There can be damage without injury, when the loss or harm was not the result of a violation of a legal duty; this is damnum absque injuria.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In The Orchard Golf & Country Club v. Yu, the Court quoted Spouses Custodio v. Court of Appeals: the mere fact that the plaintiff suffered losses does not give rise to a right to recover damages. To warrant recovery, there must be both a right of action for a legal wrong inflicted by the defendant and damage resulting to the plaintiff; wrong without damage, or damage without wrong, does not constitute a cause of action, since damages are merely part of the remedy allowed for the injury caused by a breach or wrong.
suggestedAnswer.application: So a plaintiff must show that the defendant breached a duty owed to him (injury) and that he suffered loss from it (damage); only then may the court award compensation (damages). A person who suffers loss from another's lawful act, such as a valid disciplinary suspension, has damage but no injury.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Injury is the wrong, damage is the harm, damages are the compensation; damage without injury is not compensable. **Bar trap:** do not use "damage" and "damages" interchangeably; and losses alone, however real, do not create a cause of action.

keyPoints: Injury: the illegal invasion of a legal right
Damage: the loss, hurt or harm resulting from the injury
Damages: the recompense or compensation awarded for the damage suffered
Recovery requires both a legal wrong and resulting damage
Damage without injury is damnum absque injuria, not compensable

source.caseTitle: The Orchard Golf & Country Club, Inc., et al. v. Yu and Yuhico
source.part: Decision, damages, damage and injury (quoting Spouses Custodio v. CA)
source.excerpt: x x x [T]he mere fact that the plaintiff suffered losses does not give rise to a right to recover damages. To warrant the recovery of damages, there must be both a right of action for a legal wrong inflicted by the defendant, and damage resulting to the plaintiff therefrom. Wrong without damage, or damage without wrong, does not constitute a cause of action, since damages are merely part of the remedy allowed for the injury caused by a breach or wrong. There is a material distinction between damages and injury. Injury is the illegal invasion of a legal right; damage is the loss, hurt, or harm which results from the injury; and damages are the recompense or compensation awarded for the damage suffered. Thus, there can be damage without injury in those instances in which the loss or harm was not the result of a violation of a legal duty. These situations are often called damnum absque injuria.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Two members of a private club deliberately violated its rules and insulted a club officer. After being given notice and a chance to explain, they were suspended by the board in accordance with the club's by-laws. They sued, claiming that friends avoided them and that they became the butt of jokes, and the trial court awarded each of them moral and exemplary damages and attorney's fees. Should the award stand? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The members were validly suspended, so any loss they suffered is damnum absque injuria; and their claims were supported only by self-serving declarations.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In The Orchard Golf & Country Club v. Yu, the Court held that the proper exercise of a lawful right cannot constitute a legal wrong for which an action will lie, even if it causes damage; "[o]ne who makes use of his own legal right does no injury. Qui jure suo utitur nullum damnum facit." The plaintiffs must prove by preponderance of evidence the fault or negligence of the defendants. Club membership is a privilege, subject to the club's rules.
suggestedAnswer.application: The members admitted the violations, were given due notice and opportunity to be heard, and were suspended under the by-laws; the suspension was a lawful means of protecting the club's interests. Their testimony about friends avoiding them was self-serving and uncorroborated; one even admitted his friends never said the suspension was the reason. Any mental anguish was brought upon themselves by deliberately breaking the rules.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The award should be set aside; no moral or exemplary damages, attorney's fees or costs. **Bar trap:** real hurt feelings are not enough; there must be a legal wrong. A valid exercise of a right, such as lawful discipline, gives no cause of action.

keyPoints: The suspension was valid: admitted violations, notice and hearing, compliance with the by-laws
Proper exercise of a lawful right is not a legal wrong (qui jure suo utitur nullum damnum facit)
Any loss is damnum absque injuria
The plaintiff must prove fault or negligence by preponderance of evidence; self-serving declarations are insufficient
Club membership is a privilege subject to the club's rules

source.caseTitle: The Orchard Golf & Country Club, Inc., et al. v. Yu and Yuhico
source.part: Decision, the claim for moral and exemplary damages
source.excerpt: With regard to the purported damages they incurred, respondents testified during the trial to support their respective allegations. … Apart from these self-serving declarations, respondents presented neither testimonial nor documentary evidence to bolster their claims. Worse, Yu even admitted that Freddy Lim and Atty. Benjie did not tell him that his suspension was the reason why they did not want to transact with him. … "One who makes use of his own legal right does no injury. Qui jure suo utitur nullum damnum facit. If damage results from a person's exercising his legal rights, it is damnum absque injuria." In this case, respondents failed to prove by preponderance of evidence that there is fault or negligence on the part of petitioners in order to oblige them to pay for the alleged damage sustained as a result of their suspension as Club members. Certainly, membership in the Club is a privilege. Regular members are entitled to use all the facilities and privileges of the Club, subject to its rules and regulations. As correctly pointed out by petitioners, the mental anguish respondents experienced, assuming to be true, was brought upon them by themselves for deliberately and consciously violating the rules and regulations of the Club.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In an intra-corporate case, the losing party mistakenly filed a notice of appeal with the trial court instead of a petition for review under Rule 43 with the Court of Appeals. Seven days after the 15-day period lapsed, it candidly admitted its mistake and asked the Court of Appeals for time to file the petition. May the Court of Appeals allow it? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Although the rules on the period to appeal are generally inviolable, they may be relaxed to serve substantial justice, and the circumstances here justify relaxation.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In The Orchard Golf & Country Club v. Yu, the Court held that appeal is a statutory privilege, and perfecting it within the period is mandatory and jurisdictional; but procedural rules may be waived or dispensed with to serve and achieve substantial justice, as when the appeal on its face appears absolutely meritorious or there are persuasive or compelling reasons to relieve a litigant of an injustice not commensurate with his thoughtlessness. Under A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC, the petition for review under Rule 43 must be filed within 15 days, but the Court of Appeals may grant an additional 15 days and a further extension of not more than 15 days for the most compelling reasons, showing that the period is not unyielding.
suggestedAnswer.application: The delay was only seven days; the party showed its intent to appeal by filing a notice of appeal; it candidly admitted the error and disclosed the material dates; there was no material prejudice to the other side; and the appeal was meritorious, since the adverse judgment awarded damages for a valid suspension. Unlike cases where a party persisted for months in the wrong remedy, this was an excusable mistake promptly corrected.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The Court of Appeals may and should allow the petition. **Bar trap:** liberality is the exception; it rests on short, excusable delay, candor, lack of prejudice and a meritorious appeal, not on mere inconvenience.

Rules may be relaxed to serve substantial justice: a meritorious appeal or compelling reasons

source.part: Decision, relaxation of the rules on the period to appeal
source.excerpt: Unlike LBP and Atty. Abrenica, petitioners in this case committed an excusable delay of merely seven (7) days. … In general, procedural rules setting the period for perfecting an appeal or filing a petition for review are inviolable considering that appeal is not a constitutional right but merely a statutory privilege and that perfection of an appeal in the manner and within the period permitted by law is not only mandatory but jurisdictional. However, procedural rules may be waived or dispensed with in order to serve and achieve substantial justice. Relaxation of the rules may be had when the appeal, on its face, appears to be absolutely meritorious or when there are persuasive or compelling reasons to relieve a litigant of an injustice not commensurate with the degree of thoughtlessness in not complying with the prescribed procedure. Notably, under A.M. No. 04-9-07-SC (Re: Mode of Appeal in Cases Formerly Cognizable by the Securities and Exchange Commission), while the petition for review under Rule 43 of the Rules should be filed within fifteen (15) days from notice of the decision or final order of the RTC, the CA may actually grant an additional period of fifteen (15) days within which to file the petition and a further extension of time not exceeding fifteen (15) days for the most compelling reasons. This implies that the reglementary period is neither an impregnable nor an unyielding rule.

choices.A: only that he suffered pain and suffering.
choices.B: only that the defendant's act was hurtful.
choices.C: only that the defendant had a legal right to act.
choices.D: that the injuries resulted from a breach of duty which the defendant owed to him: a concurrence of injury to the plaintiff and legal responsibility by the person causing it.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Rico, 25 years old, was killed. His mother testified that he earned ₱10,000 a month as a farm laborer. Following the formula applied in People v. Muyco, how much should be awarded to his heirs for loss of earning capacity? Show the computation.

suggestedAnswer.answer: ₱880,080.00. Net earning capacity = 2/3 × (80 − age at death) × (gross annual income − 80% of gross annual income).
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In People v. Muyco, the Court computed lost earnings using the formula 2/3 (80 − ATD [age at time of death]) × (GAI [gross annual income]) − 80% GAI, deducting 80% of the gross annual income, and awarded the heirs of a 19-year-old farm laborer earning ₱1,600 a month ₱156,172.80.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The heirs are entitled to ₱880,080.00 for loss of earning capacity. **Bar trap:** do not multiply by the full gross annual income; deduct the 80% first (as Muyco did), and use the victim's age at death, not his age at trial.

keyPoints: Formula: 2/3 × (80 − age at death) × (gross annual income − 80% of gross annual income)
Gross annual income ₱120,000; net after 80% deduction ₱24,000

source.excerpt: In the instant case, the victim was nineteen (19) years old at the time of his death and earning P1,600.00 monthly as a farm laborer. Thus — 2/3 (80-19) x (P1,600 x 12) - 80% (P1,600.00 x 12) 2/3 (61) x P19,200 - 80% (P19,200) 40.67 x [P19,200 - P15,360] 40.67 x P3,840 = P156,172.80 ==========

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In a murder case, the heirs claim damages for the victim's loss of earning capacity but present no documentary evidence, only the testimony of the victim's mother that he earned ₱1,600 a month as a farm laborer. May the court award damages for loss of earning capacity? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. As a rule, documentary evidence is needed to substantiate a claim for loss of earning capacity, but oral testimony suffices when the victim was self-employed earning less than the minimum wage, in a line of work where no documentary evidence is available, or was employed as a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In People v. Muyco, the Court quoted People v. Dizon: documentary evidence should be presented as a rule, but testimony as to the victim's earnings has sufficed (as in People v. Verde); to claim the damages without documentary evidence there must be oral testimony that (a) the victim was self-employed earning less than the minimum wage and judicial notice was taken that in the victim's line of work no documentary evidence is available, or (b) the victim was employed as a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage. In Muyco itself the Court found that the trial court failed to award these damages despite the mother's testimony, and awarded them.
suggestedAnswer.application: The victim was a farm laborer earning ₱1,600 a month, the kind of low-wage work where receipts are not usually available, and his mother testified to his earnings. That testimony is a sufficient basis for the award.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The court may award damages for loss of earning capacity based on the testimony. **Bar trap:** the exception is limited to low earners (below minimum wage) and lines of work without documentary records; a professional with higher income must ordinarily present documentary proof.

keyPoints: General rule: documentary evidence is needed for loss of earning capacity
Exception: oral testimony suffices for a self-employed victim earning below minimum wage in work without available documents
Or for a daily wage worker earning below minimum wage
In Muyco, the mother's testimony that her son earned ₱1,600 a month as a farm laborer sufficed

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: The only eyewitness to a stabbing, the victim's uncle, testified that he just stood frozen while his nephew was stabbed a meter away and was dragged off, and that the wound was on the neck, while the autopsy placed it just below the collarbone. The accused, positively identified by the witness, claims he was in another town 50 kilometers away. Should the accused be acquitted? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The witness's failure to react does not make his testimony incredible, the discrepancy on the location of the wound is minor, and the alibi fails against positive identification, especially as physical impossibility of being at the scene was not shown.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In People v. Muyco, the Court held that different people react differently to a startling or frightful experience; there is no standard behavior, and a witness's inability to move, help or run is not a ground to doubt his testimony. Discrepancies in minor details strengthen credibility, as they erase any suspicion of rehearsed testimony. Alibi cannot prevail over positive identification, and it is weaker still when the accused fails to show that it was physically impossible for him to be at the crime scene.
suggestedAnswer.application: The uncle was stunned, it being his first time to see a stabbing. To a layman, the neck and the collarbone are practically the same place. The other town was only 50 kilometers away, and no evidence showed it was impossible to travel to the crime scene; the witness had no ill motive to lie.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The accused should be convicted. **Bar trap:** "he would have shouted or helped" is not a test of credibility; and alibi requires physical impossibility, not mere distance.

keyPoints: No standard human reaction to a startling event; freezing does not impair credibility
Minor inconsistencies strengthen credibility and negate rehearsal
Positive identification by a witness without ill motive prevails over alibi
Alibi requires proof of physical impossibility of being at the scene

source.caseTitle: People v. Muyco
source.part: Decision, credibility of the eyewitness and the defense of alibi
source.excerpt: We disagree. Different people react differently to a given type of situation. There is no standard form of human behavioral response when one is confronted with a strange, startling or frightful experience. … A witness' inability to move, help or even to run away when the incident occurs is not a ground to label his testimony as doubtful and unworthy of belief. … Inconsistencies and discrepancies in the testimony of a witness on minor details only serve to strengthen the credibility of the witness. … Weak as it was, accused-appellant's alibi became all the more ineffectual when he failed to demonstrate that it was physically impossible for him to be at the crime scene at the time it was committed. He testified being in Passi, Iloilo, during the stabbing incident. Passi, Iloilo is only fifty (50) kilometers from Cabatuan, Iloilo, the place where the crime was committed. He did not offer any evidence to prove impossibility of access between the two (2) places when the crime transpired.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A bus fell into a ravine, killing a 39-year-old passenger who worked as a section chief in a government bureau. Her husband testified that she earned ₱83,088 a year; no other evidence of her income was presented. The trial court awarded ₱1,135,536 for her loss of earning capacity. (a) What damages are the heirs of a passenger who dies from a breach of contract of carriage entitled to? (b) Was the award for loss of earning capacity proper?

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) Under Article 1764 in relation to Article 2206 of the Civil Code, the carrier must pay indemnity for death, indemnity for loss of earning capacity, and moral damages. (b) No. The award for loss of earning capacity lacked documentary proof and did not fall under the exceptions, so it should be deleted; but temperate damages may be awarded instead, since some pecuniary loss was established.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Victory Liner v. Gammad, the Court held that documentary evidence is the rule for loss of earning capacity, with exceptions only when the deceased was self-employed earning less than the minimum wage (with judicial notice that no documentary evidence is available in that line of work), or employed as a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage. Under Article 2224, temperate or moderate damages, more than nominal but less than compensatory, may be recovered when the court finds that some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount cannot, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty.
suggestedAnswer.application: A government section chief earning ₱83,088 a year is neither a self-employed person nor a daily wage worker earning below the minimum wage, so her husband's testimony alone is insufficient. But that she earned an income and that her death caused her family pecuniary loss were established, so the Court awarded ₱500,000 temperate damages in lieu of the deleted award.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Death indemnity, loss of earning capacity (with proper proof) and moral damages; here, temperate damages replace the unproven loss of earning capacity. **Bar trap:** the testimonial exception is for low-wage earners only; and temperate damages are the remedy when loss is certain but its amount is not.

keyPoints: Art. 1764 with Art. 2206: indemnity for death, indemnity for loss of earning capacity, moral damages
Loss of earning capacity requires documentary evidence, except for self-employed or daily-wage earners below the minimum wage
A BIR section chief does not fall under the exceptions
Temperate damages (Art. 2224) when pecuniary loss is shown but its amount cannot be proved with certainty
₱500,000 temperate damages awarded in lieu of loss of earning capacity

source.caseTitle: Victory Liner, Inc. v. Gammad, et al.
source.part: Decision, damages for the death of a passenger and temperate damages
source.excerpt: Article 1764 in relation to Article 2206 of the Civil Code, holds the common carrier in breach of its contract of carriage that results in the death of a passenger liable to pay the following: (1) indemnity for death, (2) indemnity for loss of earning capacity, and (3) moral damages. … The award of compensatory damages for the loss of the deceased’s earning capacity should be deleted for lack of basis. As a rule, documentary evidence should be presented to substantiate the claim for damages for loss of earning capacity. By way of exception, damages for loss of earning capacity may be awarded despite the absence of documentary evidence when (1) the deceased is self-employed earning less than the minimum wage under current labor laws, and judicial notice may be taken of the fact that in the deceased’s line of work no documentary evidence is available; or (2) the deceased is employed as a daily wage worker earning less than the minimum wage under current labor laws. … The award is clearly erroneous because the deceased’s earnings does not fall within the exceptions. However, the fact of loss having been established, temperate damages in the amount of P500,000.00 should be awarded to respondents. Under Article 2224 of the Civil Code, temperate or moderate damages, which are more than nominal but less than compensatory damages, may be recovered when the court finds that some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount can not, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In a suit for the death of a bus passenger, the trial court awarded ₱400,000 as "exemplary and moral damages" in one lump sum, and actual damages based on a handwritten list of funeral expenses and a contract for the construction of the tomb, in addition to official receipts. Are these awards proper? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Moral and exemplary damages cannot be lumped together, and actual damages must be supported by competent proof such as official receipts; a list of expenses and a construction contract are not enough.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Victory Liner v. Gammad, the Court held that moral and exemplary damages are based on different jural foundations and require separate determination. In breach of contract, moral damages are recovered when the defendant acted in bad faith or with gross negligence, or when the breach itself constitutes a tort resulting in physical injuries; and by special rule (Article 1764 with Article 2206) when a passenger dies. Exemplary damages may be recovered in contractual obligations if the defendant acted in a wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive or malevolent manner; a carrier that fails to prove extraordinary diligence is presumed to have acted recklessly. Following People v. Duban, only substantiated and proven expenses, genuinely incurred in connection with the death, wake or burial, are recognized.
suggestedAnswer.application: The Court separately awarded ₱100,000 moral damages (for the heirs' grief) and ₱100,000 exemplary damages (the carrier being presumed reckless), and reduced the actual damages to ₱78,160, the amount supported by official receipts, rejecting the list of expenses and the tomb contract.

source.excerpt: Anent the award of moral damages, the same cannot be lumped with exemplary damages because they are based on different jural foundations. In culpa contractual or breach of contract, moral damages may be recovered when the defendant acted in bad faith or was guilty of gross negligence (amounting to bad faith) or in wanton disregard of contractual obligations and, as in this case, when the act of breach of contract itself constitutes the tort that results in physical injuries. By special rule in Article 1764 in relation to Article 2206 of the Civil Code, moral damages may also be awarded in case the death of a passenger results from a breach of carriage. On the other hand, exemplary damages, which are awarded by way of example or correction for the public good may be recovered in contractual obligations if the defendant acted in wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive, or malevolent manner. … The actual damages awarded by the trial court reduced by the Court of Appeals should be further reduced. Duban, it was held that only substantiated and proven expenses or those that appear to have been genuinely incurred in connection with the death, wake or burial of the victim will be recognized. questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A bus company sued for a passenger's death lost because its lawyer missed hearings, so it was deemed to have waived cross-examination and the presentation of its evidence; the lawyer had filed an answer, a pre-trial brief and a timely appeal. The company now claims denial of due process, and also that the accident was purely accidental after 50 years of safe operation. Rule on both claims.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Both fail. The negligence of counsel binds the client, and this was not gross negligence amounting to a denial of due process. And the company did not overcome the presumption that it was at fault for the passenger's death.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Victory Liner v. Gammad, the Court held that a counsel's acts within his authority are the client's acts, so his negligence binds the client; the exceptions are reckless or gross negligence that deprives the client of due process, or that results in outright deprivation of liberty or property, or when the interests of justice so require. Due process guards against the denial of the opportunity to be heard. On the merits, a common carrier must carry passengers safely as far as human care and foresight can provide, using the utmost diligence of very cautious persons; when a passenger dies or is injured, the carrier is presumed at fault, and the presumption may only be overcome by evidence of extraordinary diligence.
suggestedAnswer.application: The company had its day in court: its lawyer filed pleadings, had the default lifted, and appealed on time; and the company itself ignored three notices of pre-trial, so it shared the fault. No evidence rebutted the presumption of negligence; a long safe record is not proof of extraordinary diligence on the day of the accident.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: No denial of due process, and the carrier is liable for breach of contract of carriage. **Bar trap:** "my lawyer was negligent" works only for gross negligence that deprives the client of due process; and a common carrier is presumed negligent, unlike a defendant in quasi-delict.

keyPoints: Negligence of counsel binds the client
Exceptions: reckless or gross negligence depriving the client of due process, outright deprivation of liberty or property, or when justice requires
Due process is the opportunity to be heard, which the company had
Common carriers: utmost diligence of very cautious persons; presumed at fault when a passenger dies
The presumption is overcome only by proof of extraordinary diligence

source.caseTitle: Victory Liner, Inc. v. Gammad, et al.
source.part: Decision, negligence of counsel and breach of contract of carriage
source.excerpt: It is settled that the negligence of counsel binds the client. This is based on the rule that any act performed by a counsel within the scope of his general or implied authority is regarded as an act of his client. Consequently, the mistake or negligence of counsel may result in the rendition of an unfavorable judgment against the client. However, the application of the general rule to a given case should be looked into and adopted according to the surrounding circumstances obtaining. Thus, exceptions to the foregoing have been recognized by the court in cases where reckless or gross negligence of counsel deprives the client of due process of law, or when its application will result in outright deprivation of the client’s liberty or property or where the interests of justice so require, and accord relief to the client who suffered by reason of the lawyer’s gross or palpable mistake or negligence. … Anent the second issue, petitioner was correctly found liable for breach of contract of carriage. A common carrier is bound to carry its passengers safely as far as human care and foresight can provide, using the utmost diligence of very cautious persons, with due regard to all the circumstances. In a contract of carriage, it is presumed that the common carrier was at fault or was negligent when a passenger dies or is injured. Unless the presumption is rebutted, the court need not even make an express finding of fault or negligence on the part of the common carrier. This statutory presumption may only be overcome by evidence that the carrier exercised extraordinary diligence.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Ramon, 50 years old, operated a hardware store and was killed in a vehicular accident through a bus driver's negligence. His heirs proved by his income tax documents that his gross annual income was ₱600,000; there is no evidence of his business expenses or living expenses. Following Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee, compute the indemnity for his loss of earning capacity.

suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee, the Court held that indemnity for loss of earning capacity under Article 2206 is awarded not for loss of earnings but for loss of capacity to earn money, and that only net earnings are considered: the earnings less expenses necessary to produce them, less living and other incidental expenses. Absent documentary evidence of expenses, it pegged necessary business expenses at 80% of the gross income and living expenses at 50% of the net income, using: Net Earning Capacity = 2/3 (80 − age at death) × (Gross Annual Income − necessary expenses), less living expenses.
suggestedAnswer.application: Life expectancy: 2/3 × (80 − 50) = 2/3 × 30 = 20 years. Gross annual income ₱600,000, less 80% necessary expenses (₱480,000) = ₱120,000. Less living expenses of 50% (₱60,000) = ₱60,000. Net earning capacity: 20 × ₱60,000 = ₱1,200,000.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The heirs are entitled to ₱1,200,000. **Bar trap:** for a business owner, deduct first the expenses necessary to earn the income, then living expenses; never multiply the gross income by the life expectancy. (Compare People v. Muyco, where 80% of the gross income of a farm laborer was deducted as living expenses.)

keyPoints: Art. 2206 indemnity is for loss of capacity to earn, not loss of earnings
Only net earnings: gross income less necessary expenses, less living expenses
Absent evidence: necessary expenses at 80% of gross; living expenses at 50% of net

source.caseTitle: Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee
source.part: Decision, computation of loss of earning capacity (net earnings)
source.excerpt: The indemnity for loss of earning capacity of the deceased is provided for by Article 2206 of the Civil Code. Compensation of this nature is awarded not for loss of earnings, but for loss of capacity to earn money. … In the computation of loss of earning capacity, only net earnings, not gross earnings, are to be considered; that is, the total of the earnings less expenses necessary for the creation of such earnings or income, less living and other incidental expenses. In the absence of documentary evidence, it is reasonable to peg necessary expenses for the lease and operation of the gasoline station at 80 percent of the gross income, and peg living expenses at 50 percent of the net income (gross income less necessary expenses). In this case, the computation for loss of earning capacity is as follows: Net Earning Capacity = Life Expectancy [2/3 (80-age at the time of death)] x Gross Annual Income (GAI) – Reasonable and Necessary Expenses (80% of GAI) X = [2/3 (80-65)] x ₱1,000,000.00 - ₱800,000.00 X = 2/3 (15) x ₱200,000.00 - ₱100,000.00(Living Expenses) X = 30/3 x ₱100,000.00 X = 10 x ₱100,000.00 X = ₱1,000,000.00

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A bus driver saw a motorcycle ahead on the left side of the highway but kept his speed and veered left, hitting the motorcycle and a parked jeep. Sued with the driver, the bus company proves that the driver passed NBI clearance, a certification from his previous employer, a physical examination, a driving test and reviews of his driving skill every six months. The driver admitted prior sideswiping incidents, which the company did not know about. (a) Was the driver negligent? (b) Is the company liable?

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) Yes; the driver failed to take the precaution an ordinary reasonable person would have taken against a foreseeable risk. (b) Yes; the company did not overcome the presumption that it failed to exercise the diligence of a good father of a family in the selection and supervision of its driver.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee, the Court held that foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence: a defendant is negligent if he acted or failed to act in such a way that an ordinary reasonable man would have realized that certain interests of certain persons were unreasonably subjected to a general but definite class of risks. Whenever an employee's negligence causes damage, there instantly arises a presumption that the employer failed to exercise due diligence in the selection or supervision of its employees; to avoid liability the employer must present convincing proof of that diligence.
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Having seen the motorcycle ahead, the driver should have slowed down; instead he kept his speed and veered into the left lane. (b) The company's tests focused only on driving ability and physical fitness; it did not sufficiently inculcate discipline and correct road behavior, and did not even know of the driver's sideswiping history. That is not convincing proof of diligence in supervision.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The driver was negligent and the company is solidarily liable. **Bar trap:** passing hiring tests (selection) does not prove diligent supervision; the employer must show both.

keyPoints: Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence
The driver saw the motorcycle but did not slow down and veered left
An employee's negligence raises a presumption of the employer's negligence in selection or supervision
The employer must overcome it by convincing proof
Tests limited to driving ability and fitness, and ignorance of prior incidents, do not suffice

source.caseTitle: Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee
source.part: Decision, negligence of the driver and liability of the employer
source.excerpt: Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence. To be negligent, a defendant must have acted or failed to act in such a way that an ordinary reasonable man would have realized that certain interests of certain persons were unreasonably subjected to a general but definite class of risks. In this case, the bus driver, who was driving on the right side of the road, already saw the motorcycle on the left side of the road before the collision. However, he did not take the necessary precaution to slow down, but drove on and bumped the motorcycle, and also the passenger jeep parked on the left side of the road, showing that the bus was negligent in veering to the left lane, causing it to hit the motorcycle and the passenger jeep. Whenever an employee’s negligence causes damage or injury to another, there instantly arises a presumption that the employer failed to exercise the due diligence of a good father of the family in the selection or supervision of its employees. To avoid liability for a quasi-delict committed by his employee, an employer must overcome the presumption by presenting convincing proof that he exercised the care and diligence of a good father of a family in the selection and supervision of his employee. The Court upholds the finding of the trial court and the Court of Appeals that petitioner is liable to respondent, since it failed to exercise the diligence of a good father of the family in the selection and supervision of its bus driver, Margarito Avila, for having failed to sufficiently inculcate in him discipline and correct behavior on the road. Indeed, petitioner’s tests were concentrated on the ability to drive and physical fitness to do so. It also did not know that Avila had been previously involved in sideswiping incidents.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Only the defendant bus company appealed a judgment awarding the plaintiff loss of earning capacity, funeral expenses and moral damages for her husband's death. The Court of Appeals added civil indemnity for the death, temperate damages for her damaged motorcycle (whose repair cost was shown only by a job estimate), and moral damages for her own physical injuries, all of which she had prayed for in her complaint. The company argues that the plaintiff did not appeal. Was the Court of Appeals correct? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. An appellate court may review matters not assigned as errors if their consideration is necessary for a just decision, and each added award had a legal basis.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee, the Court applied Section 8, Rule 51 of the Rules of Civil Procedure: errors not assigned may be considered if they affect jurisdiction or the validity of the judgment, are closely related to or dependent on an assigned error, or are plain or clerical errors; and the appellate court is clothed with ample authority to review matters not assigned if necessary to arrive at a just decision. Civil indemnity for death is proper under Article 2206; temperate damages may be recovered under Article 2224 when some pecuniary loss is shown but its amount cannot be proved with certainty; and moral damages may be recovered in quasi-delicts causing physical injuries under Article 2219.
suggestedAnswer.application: The trial court overlooked damages the plaintiff had prayed for. The damage to the motorcycle was certainly caused by the driver's negligence, but a job estimate is not competent proof of its actual cost, so ₱10,000 temperate damages was reasonable. The plaintiff's own injuries supported moral damages (reduced by the Supreme Court to ₱30,000 per prevailing jurisprudence), and the death supported ₱50,000 civil indemnity.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The Court of Appeals was correct. **Bar trap:** the general rule that only assigned errors are reviewed has exceptions; and a job estimate supports temperate, not actual, damages.

keyPoints: Sec. 8, Rule 51: unassigned errors may be considered in certain cases
The appellate court may review matters not assigned if necessary for a just decision
Civil indemnity for death (Art. 2206)
Temperate damages when loss is certain but its amount unproven (Art. 2224); a job estimate is not proof of actual cost
Moral damages for physical injuries in quasi-delicts (Art. 2219)

source.caseTitle: Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee
source.part: Decision, damages awarded on appeal though not assigned as errors
source.excerpt: In addition, the Court of Appeals correctly awarded temperate damages in the amount of ₱10,000.00 for the damage caused on respondent’s motorcycle. Under Art. 2224 of the Civil Code, temperate damages "may be recovered when the court finds that some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount cannot, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty." The cost of the repair of the motorcycle was prayed for by respondent in her Complaint. However, the evidence presented was merely a job estimate of the cost of the motorcycle’s repair amounting to ₱17, 829.00. … The Court of Appeals also correctly awarded respondent moral damages for the physical injuries she sustained due to the vehicular accident. Under Art. 2219 of the Civil Code, moral damages may be recovered in quasi-delicts causing physical injuries. … Further, the Court of Appeals correctly awarded respondent civil indemnity for the death of her husband, which has been fixed by current jurisprudence at ₱50,000.00. The award is proper under Art. 2206 of the Civil Code. In fine, the Court of Appeals correctly awarded civil indemnity for the death of respondent’s husband, temperate damages, and moral damages for the physical injuries sustained by respondent in addition to the damages granted by the trial court to respondent. The trial court overlooked awarding the additional damages, which were prayed for by respondent in her Amended Complaint. The appellate court is clothed with ample authority to review matters, even if they are not assigned as errors in the appeal, if it finds that their consideration is necessary in arriving at a just decision of the case.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old employee earning ₱20,000 a month, as shown by his payslips, was murdered. The trial court awarded actual, moral and exemplary damages and civil indemnity, but nothing for loss of earning capacity, since the heirs did not appeal. Following People v. Asilan, may the appellate court award it, and how much?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Under Article 2206, the defendant is liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, which in every case shall be assessed and awarded by the court. Computed as in Asilan: ₱3,600,000.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In People v. Asilan, the Court held that both lower courts failed to consider that under Article 2206 the accused is also liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, payable to his heirs, and awarded it on appeal. It used: Net Earning Capacity = life expectancy × (gross annual income − living expenses) = 2/3 (80 − age at death) × (gross annual income − 50% of gross annual income), net income being gross income less living expenses.
suggestedAnswer.application: Life expectancy: 2/3 × (80 − 35) = 2/3 × 45 = 30 years. Gross annual income: ₱20,000 × 12 = ₱240,000. Less 50% living expenses (₱120,000) = ₱120,000. Net earning capacity: 30 × ₱120,000 = ₱3,600,000. The payslips satisfy the requirement of documentary proof.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The appellate court should award ₱3,600,000 for loss of earning capacity. **Bar trap:** the award is mandatory under Article 2206 when proven, even if the trial court overlooked it; and the living-expense deduction used in Asilan (50% of gross) differs from that used in Muyco (80% of gross), so follow the facts and the approach of the decision cited.

keyPoints: Art. 2206: liability for loss of earning capacity, assessed and awarded by the court in every case
The appellate court may award it even if the lower courts failed to
Formula used in Asilan: 2/3 (80 − age) × (gross annual income − 50% living expenses)
Documentary proof of income (payslips) supports the award

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What are the factors in computing the damages recoverable for the loss of earning capacity of a deceased person? When may such indemnity NOT be awarded under Article 2206 of the Civil Code? Explain, following People v. Asilan.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The factors are: (1) the number of years on the basis of which the damages shall be computed, using the formula 2/3 × (80 − age of the deceased at death) = life expectancy, adopted from the American Expectancy Table of Mortality; and (2) the rate at which the losses sustained by the heirs should be fixed, that is, the net income (gross income less living expenses). The indemnity is not awarded when the deceased, on account of permanent physical disability not caused by the defendant, had no earning capacity at the time of his death.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: People v. Asilan quoted Article 2206: the amount of damages for death caused by a crime or quasi-delict shall be at least three thousand pesos, even if there are mitigating circumstances; in addition, (1) the defendant shall be liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, paid to the heirs, and such indemnity shall in every case be assessed and awarded by the court, unless the deceased on account of permanent physical disability not caused by the defendant had no earning capacity at the time of his death. The Court then listed the two factors.
suggestedAnswer.application: So in every death caused by a crime or quasi-delict, the court must determine the deceased's life expectancy and net income, unless he had no earning capacity because of a permanent disability not caused by the defendant (for example, if he was already permanently incapacitated from an earlier, unrelated cause).
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Two factors: life expectancy and net income; the only exception is lack of earning capacity due to a permanent disability not caused by the defendant. **Bar trap:** a disability caused by the defendant himself does not excuse him from this indemnity.

keyPoints: Factor 1: number of years, life expectancy = 2/3 × (80 − age at death), from the American Expectancy Table of Mortality
Factor 2: the rate of loss, net income = gross income less living expenses
Art. 2206: indemnity shall in every case be assessed and awarded by the court
Exception: the deceased had no earning capacity because of a permanent physical disability not caused by the defendant

source.caseTitle: People v. Asilan
source.part: Discussion, loss of earning capacity (the factors and Article 2206)
source.excerpt: Art. 2206. The amount of damages for death caused by a crime or quasi-delict shall be at least three thousand pesos, even though there may have been mitigating circumstances. In addition: (1) The defendant shall be liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, and the indemnity shall be paid to the heirs of the latter; such indemnity shall in every case be assessed and awarded by the court, unless the deceased on account of permanent physical disability not caused by the defendant, had no earning capacity at the time of his death; … The following are the factors in computing the amount of damages recoverable for the loss of earning capacity of the deceased: 1) The number of years on the basis of which the damages shall be computed. This is based on the formula (2/3 x 80 – age of the deceased at the time of his death = life expectancy), which is adopted from the American Expectancy Table of Mortality; and 2) The rate at which the losses sustained by the heirs of the deceased should be fixed. Net income is arrived at by deducting the amount of the victim’s living expenses from the amount of his gross income.

Asilan, the Court increased civil indemnity and moral damages "[p]ursuant to prevailing jurisprudence"; awarded exemplary damages "in view of the presence of the qualifying circumstance of treachery" under Article 2230 of the Civil Code; fixed actual damages on the widow's receipts for hospital and funeral expenses; and applied Article 2206 for loss of earning capacity.

Candaza, an Information lacking essential allegations may still sustain a conviction when the accused fails to object during trial and the deficiency is cured by competent evidence. **A and B are wrong** for those reasons. **D is wrong:** the Court reiterated that qualifying circumstances must be properly pleaded. **Bar trap:** object to a defective Information before pleading, or the objection is generally waived.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Distinguish attorney's fees awarded as an item of damages under Article 2208 of the Civil Code from the attorney's fees that a lawyer claims from his own client for professional services, as explained in Quirante v. Intermediate Appellate Court.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Attorney's fees under Article 2208 are an item of damages awarded in favor of the litigant, not of his counsel; the litigant is the judgment creditor who may enforce them by execution against the losing party. Attorney's fees for professional services, on the other hand, arise from the contract between the lawyer and the client, with the lawyer as creditor and the client as debtor.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Quirante v. IAC, the Court held that what the petitioners claimed as attorney's fees was "different from attorney's fees as an item of damages provided for under Article 2208 of the Civil Code, wherein the award is made in favor of the litigant, not of his counsel, and the litigant, not his counsel, is the judgment creditor who may enforce the judgment for attorney's fees by execution." The petitioners' claims were based on an alleged contract for professional services.
suggestedAnswer.application: Thus the ₱30,000 attorney's fees awarded against the contractor and its surety in the main judgment belonged to the client as damages, while Atty. Quirante's claim for a share of the recovery under his agreement with the client was a separate claim against the client and his heirs.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Article 2208 fees go to the client and are paid by the losing party; professional fees go to the lawyer and are paid by the client. **Bar trap:** a lawyer cannot treat the Article 2208 award as automatically his own; it is the client's damages.

keyPoints: Art. 2208 attorney's fees: an item of damages awarded to the litigant, who is the judgment creditor
Paid by the losing party; enforceable by the litigant through execution
Fees for professional services: based on the lawyer-client contract
There the lawyer is the creditor and the client the debtor
